blocks.text: A confidence interval reports a range of plausible values for a population parameter, rather than a single point estimate, and states how confident that range is likely to contain the truth. It is the standard way of honestly communicating the uncertainty that the sampling lesson showed is unavoidable whenever conclusions are drawn from a sample rather than a full population.

blocks.caption: The core ideas this lesson connects together

blocks.text: 1. What a Confidence Interval Reports

A point estimate, like a sample mean, is a single best guess for a population parameter. A confidence interval instead reports a range, such as 68 to 74, along with a confidence level, such as 95 percent, expressing how much uncertainty surrounds that single guess.
This range-plus-confidence-level format is the standard way statisticians communicate an estimate honestly, since a bare point estimate on its own gives no sense of how much it might be off.

This directly builds on the sampling distribution concept from the sampling lesson, a confidence interval is essentially a practical, usable slice cut from that theoretical distribution of possible sample means.

This same logic extends beyond means and proportions to almost any statistic worth reporting, correlation coefficients, regression slopes, and model performance metrics can all be given a confidence interval using the same underlying philosophy.
2. The Confidence Level

A 95 percent confidence level means that if the same sampling procedure were repeated many times, about 95 percent of the resulting intervals would contain the true population parameter. It is a statement about the reliability of the method used to build the interval, not a probability statement about any single already-computed interval.

blocks.title: A concrete example
blocks.content: It is a common misreading to say a 95 percent confidence interval means there is a 95 percent chance the true mean lies in this specific range. The more precise statement is that the procedure used to build the interval captures the true mean 95 percent of the time across repeated sampling, the specific interval either does or does not contain it, with no probability left to assign after the fact.

blocks.text: This subtlety trips up even experienced practitioners, the confidence level describes the long run behavior of the procedure across many hypothetical repeated samples, not the odds attached to the one interval sitting in front of you right now.

A useful mental model, imagine running the exact same study 100 times, each time drawing a fresh sample and building a new 95 percent interval, roughly 95 of those 100 intervals would end up containing the true population parameter.

Choosing a confidence level before collecting data, rather than after seeing the results, keeps the interpretation honest and avoids the temptation to pick whichever level happens to make a result look most favorable.
3. The Formula for a Confidence Interval

A confidence interval for a mean is built as sample mean plus or minus (critical value times standard error), where standard error is the standard deviation of the sampling distribution introduced in the sampling lesson, and the critical value comes from a normal or t-distribution matching the chosen confidence level.

code.content:
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats
data = np.array([68, 71, 69, 74, 70, 72, 68, 73])
mean = np.mean(data)
std_err = stats.sem(data)   # standard error of the mean
ci = stats.t.interval(0.95, len(data)-1, loc=mean, scale=std_err)
print(ci)

blocks.text: The critical value scales the standard error up to match whatever confidence level was chosen, a larger critical value stretches the interval wider to capture the truth more often across repeated sampling.
scipy stats.t.interval handles both the critical value lookup and the final interval construction in a single call, sparing the need to manually look up a critical value from a statistical table.
4. Standard Error

Standard error measures how much a sample mean is expected to vary from sample to sample, computed as the sample standard deviation divided by the square root of the sample size. Larger samples produce a smaller standard error, and therefore a narrower, more precise confidence interval.

code.content:
sample_std = np.std(data, ddof=1)
n = len(data)
standard_error = sample_std / np.sqrt(n)
print(standard_error)

blocks.text: Standard error should not be confused with the plain sample standard deviation, standard deviation measures spread within a single sample, while standard error measures how much the sample mean itself would vary across many different samples.

This distinction, standard deviation describing one sample versus standard error describing the variability of an estimate across many hypothetical samples, is worth keeping firmly separate whenever reading a research paper or a model evaluation report.
5. Wider Sample, Narrower Interval

Because standard error shrinks as sample size grows, a larger sample produces a tighter, more informative confidence interval at the same confidence level. This is a direct, practical payoff of the law of large numbers introduced in the sampling lesson.

code.content:
for n in [10, 100, 1000]:
    sample = np.random.normal(70, 5, n)
    ci_width = stats.t.interval(0.95, n-1, loc=np.mean(sample), scale=stats.sem(sample))
    print(n, ci_width[1] - ci_width[0])   # interval width shrinks as n grows

blocks.text: Because standard error shrinks with the square root of sample size, quadrupling the sample size only halves the interval width, a diminishing returns pattern worth remembering when deciding how much extra data collection is actually worth the cost.

This relationship is exactly why doubling a survey budget rarely doubles the precision of its results, the square root relationship means the payoff from additional data collection shrinks steadily the more has already been gathered.
6. Confidence Level Versus Interval Width

Choosing a higher confidence level, 99 percent instead of 95 percent, widens the interval, since being more certain of capturing the truth requires casting a wider net. There is a fundamental tradeoff between how confident an interval is and how precise it is.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Confidence level","Effect on interval width"],"rows":[["90 percent","narrowest of the three, least conservative"],["95 percent","the most common default choice"],["99 percent","widest, most conservative, most likely to contain the truth"]]}

blocks.text: Choosing 95 percent as a default is largely convention rather than a strict mathematical requirement, some fields, particularly ones where a wrong conclusion is very costly, prefer a stricter 99 percent standard instead.
Medical and safety critical fields often lean toward stricter confidence levels precisely because the cost of a wrong conclusion there is far higher than in a low stakes marketing experiment.
7. Confidence Intervals for Proportions
Confidence intervals also apply to proportions, such as the fraction of users who click a button, using a formula built around the standard error of a proportion rather than a mean.

code.content:
from statsmodels.stats.proportion import proportion_confint
successes = 62
trials = 200
ci = proportion_confint(successes, trials, alpha=0.05, method="normal")
print(ci)

blocks.text: This exact formula is what powers a reported click through rate confidence interval in an A/B test dashboard, letting a team judge whether an observed difference between two variants is likely real or could simply be sampling noise.

Proportions have their own standard error formula, built from the observed proportion itself rather than a separately measured standard deviation, since the spread of a yes or no outcome is determined entirely by the proportion value.
8. Bootstrapped Confidence Intervals

When the underlying formula for standard error is unavailable or unreliable, a bootstrapped confidence interval can be built directly by resampling the data with replacement, covered in the sampling lesson, many times, computing the statistic on each resample, and reading off percentiles from the resulting distribution.

code.content:
boot_means = [np.random.choice(data, size=len(data), replace=True).mean() for _ in range(10000)]
ci_lower = np.percentile(boot_means, 2.5)
ci_upper = np.percentile(boot_means, 97.5)
print(ci_lower, ci_upper)

blocks.text: Bootstrapping is especially useful for statistics that do not have a simple, well known standard error formula, such as a median or a correlation coefficient, where resampling sidesteps the need for a closed form equation entirely.

Reading the interval directly off the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the bootstrapped distribution, as shown here, is called the percentile method, one of several bootstrap confidence interval variants used in practice.
9. Confidence Intervals in AI Practice

items: Reporting a model accuracy as 87 percent with a 95 percent confidence interval of 84 to 90 percent communicates far more honestly than the bare number alone, since accuracy measured on a test set is itself a sample statistic.

A/B testing for a new feature or model version reports the observed lift alongside a confidence interval to judge whether an improvement is statistically meaningful or could plausibly be random noise.

Cross validation, which trains and evaluates a model on several different data splits, produces multiple performance estimates that can be summarized with a confidence interval rather than a single, potentially misleading number.

blocks.text: These use cases share a common thread, whenever a single number is reported as if it were the exact truth, a confidence interval is the standard tool for expressing how much that number should actually be trusted.

Model cards and research papers increasingly report confidence intervals alongside headline metrics specifically to prevent readers from overinterpreting small, potentially noisy differences between competing systems.
10. Z Interval Versus T Interval

When the population standard deviation is known, or the sample is very large, a confidence interval uses the normal, or z, distribution for its critical value. When the population standard deviation is unknown and must be estimated from a small sample, the t-distribution is used instead, since it has heavier tails that widen the interval slightly to account for the extra uncertainty of estimating spread from limited data.

code.content:
from scipy import stats
n = 8
critical_z = stats.norm.ppf(0.975)
critical_t = stats.t.ppf(0.975, df=n-1)
print(critical_z, critical_t)   # t critical value is slightly larger, widening the interval

blocks.text: As sample size grows large, typically past around 30, the t-distribution converges toward the normal distribution, making the difference between the two approaches negligible for large samples.
11. Confidence Intervals and Sample Size Planning

Before collecting data, the confidence interval formula can be rearranged to estimate how large a sample is needed to achieve a desired margin of error, a common practical question when planning a survey or an experiment.

code.content:
desired_margin = 2
assumed_std = 10
confidence_z = 1.96   # for 95 percent confidence
required_n = (confidence_z * assumed_std / desired_margin) ** 2
print(round(required_n))   # roughly how many samples are needed

blocks.text: This calculation always requires an upfront guess about the underlying spread of the data, often taken from a smaller pilot study or from historical measurements, since the true standard deviation is not yet known before the main study is even run.

Underestimating the assumed standard deviation during this planning stage leads to a sample that ends up too small once real data is collected, forcing an uncomfortable choice between accepting a wider than desired interval or gathering more data later.
12. A Worked Example

A model is evaluated on 8 different random test splits, giving accuracy scores of 0.85, 0.87, 0.83, 0.88, 0.86, 0.84, 0.89, 0.85. Compute a 95 percent confidence interval for the true average accuracy.

code.content:
scores = np.array([0.85, 0.87, 0.83, 0.88, 0.86, 0.84, 0.89, 0.85])
mean = np.mean(scores)
ci = stats.t.interval(0.95, len(scores)-1, loc=mean, scale=stats.sem(scores))
print(mean, ci)

blocks.text: Reporting the accuracy this way, as a range rather than a single 0.858, communicates directly that a slightly different set of 8 test splits could plausibly have produced anywhere from about 0.844 to 0.872, a far more honest picture than the bare average alone.
This same technique generalizes directly to comparing two different models by looking at whether their accuracy confidence intervals overlap substantially or sit clearly apart from one another.
13. Common Mistakes

items: Misinterpreting a 95 percent confidence interval as a 95 percent probability that the true parameter lies in that specific already-computed range, the correct interpretation is about the long run reliability of the method.
Reporting only a point estimate without any interval, hiding how much uncertainty is actually present in a small sample.
Using a normal distribution based interval on a very small sample, where a t-distribution based interval, which accounts for the extra uncertainty of a small sample, is the more appropriate choice.
Assuming a narrower interval always means a better result, a narrow interval from a biased sample can still be confidently wrong.

blocks.text: A related trap worth naming directly: comparing two overlapping confidence intervals and concluding there is no meaningful difference between them, overlapping intervals do not automatically mean the underlying difference is not statistically significant, a proper hypothesis test is the more reliable way to answer that question directly.

It is also easy to forget that a confidence interval only accounts for sampling variability, it says nothing about other sources of error like a flawed measurement instrument or a biased data collection process.
14. Practice: Build a Confidence Interval
Given the dataset [22, 25, 21, 24, 23, 26, 22, 25], compute the sample mean, standard error, and a 90 percent confidence interval.

code.content:
data = np.array([22, 25, 21, 24, 23, 26, 22, 25])
mean = np.mean(data)
ci_90 = stats.t.interval(0.90, len(data)-1, loc=mean, scale=stats.sem(data))
print(mean, ci_90)

blocks.text: Compare the width of this 90 percent interval against what a 95 percent interval on the same data would produce, confirming directly that the higher confidence level widens the range, exactly as section 6 describes.
Try recomputing this interval using the bootstrap percentile method from section 8 instead of the t-distribution formula, and compare how closely the two approaches agree on this small dataset.
Key Takeaway

Sample size planning, from section 11, is the practical question every experiment design eventually has to answer, collecting too little data produces an interval too wide to be useful, while collecting far more than needed wastes time and resources.

A confidence interval expresses a range of plausible values for a population parameter, built from a point estimate, a standard error, and a chosen confidence level, always trading off precision against certainty. It is the honest, standard way to communicate the uncertainty inherent in every sample based estimate, from a survey result to a reported model accuracy.

The hypothesis testing lesson immediately ahead uses this exact same machinery, standard error and sampling distributions, to answer a related but different question, not what range a parameter likely falls in, but whether the evidence supports rejecting a specific claim about it.

The z versus t distinction from section 10 is worth remembering specifically, defaulting to a z interval on a small sample understates the true uncertainty, producing an interval that looks more precise than it actually is.
